newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-OFFICIALS PROMISE SERIOUS SERIES SECURITY.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-OFFICIALS PROMISE SERIOUS SERIES SECURITY.

text.p: New York officials promised Friday to crack down on the possible mayhem at baseball's World Series -- ticket-scalping and field-crashing -- at Yankee Stadium this weekend.

Yankees fans have been known to hurl batteries, tennis balls and obscenities at opposing players. This championship series has seen its share of bad behaviour and as the deciding game will be played in Yankee Stadium, the city is bracing itself.

In the first game between the Yankees and the Atlanta Braves last Sunday in Yankee Stadium, New York City police handed out 121 summonses for ticket scalping, 22 for disorderly conduct, 47 for illegal peddling, 20 for carrying an open alcohol container and five for forgery.
Four fans on Sunday and seven fans on Monday who stormed the field were issued summonses for trespassing -- much to the ire of Mayor Rudolph Giuliani.
The mayor blasted police for not arresting the unruly fans and vowed stiffer penalties to anyone else who dared to promote the city's lawless image.
Giuliani said at a news conference on Friday that he hoped fans would be too intrigued by a "very close game that keeps their interest" to misbehave.
As a back-up plan, he said he has instructed more police to patrol the stadium, taking more responsibilities from the stadium's private security.

New York State Attorney General Dennis Vacco announced that he filed three lawsuits Friday in Manhattan State Supreme Court against three ticket scalping agencies, which resold tickets for prices ranging from $250 to $1,500, he said.
"This lawsuit serves as a brushback pitch to any individual or entity intending to line their pockets by scalping tickets to sporting events, shows or concerts in New York," Vacco said.
